Explanation:
[A|Inquiry Relevance] Round 1 Student selected a question probing whether the John Deere settlement creates innovation disincentives — directly serving the stated intent to investigate "legal precedents and implications of hardware technology innovations." Round 2 shifted to Amgen enablement's application to hardware subsectors, and Round 3 to the DRAM prior-art combination and the eligibility-vs-obviousness distribution. Each selection tracks the user's evolving guidance ("Recent legal cases... involving hardware technology innovations" → "investigate the legal precedents and implications") and builds on prior rounds rather than restarting. The questions are technically precise and consequential, though Round 3's second question (eligibility vs. obviousness distribution) was acknowledged as unmeasurable, slightly limiting its payoff.

[A|Perspective Expansion] Round 1 Instructor reframed the Deere case as antitrust/aftermarket rather than product liability: "the case is not a product-liability precedent... A company reading this settlement is not being told 'your software might injure someone, so pay up.'" This is a genuine reframing of how the case's innovation effects operate. Round 2 developed the claim-scope vs. technology-category distinction in Amgen, noting "the distinction is evidentiary and practical, not doctrinal." Round 3 added the two-front structure (eligibility vs. obviousness) and the standards-of-review asymmetry. These are consequential perspectives connected to the user's goal, though the empirical-validation angle (Round 1's second question) remained largely hypothetical.

[A|Evidence-Based Progress] Round 1 Instructor distinguished the settlement's legal theory from liability expansion and specified structured remedies (tiered repair categories, FRAND-style licensing) as alternatives, bounding the innovation-chill concern. Round 2 grounded the Amgen analysis in the actual holding ("26 antibodies and two screening methods... claimed an entire genus") and explicitly flagged "There is no clean reported decision that expressly draws a semiconductor-versus-mechanical enablement line." Round 3 identified the Netlist case specifics (No. 2024-1707, Sept. 2, 2026, U.S. Patent No. 10,949,339) and the substantial-evidence standard, while honestly noting the public excerpts don't reproduce the exact prior-art mapping. The PTAB selection-bias caveat ("nearly half of petitions are rejected before the technical merits") productively bounds an empirical claim. Support is visible and appropriately qualified; source passages were not independently verified here.

[A|Incremental Value] Chronologically: Round 1 delivered a reframing of Deere as antitrust (not liability) plus a concrete remedy menu and an empirical-validation design (panel linking PTAB outcomes to R&D proxies). Round 2 added the Amgen claim-scope principle applied to hardware and the Deere compliance-line analysis with its unresolved gap ("neither the FTC order nor the private settlements publish a bright-line test"). Round 3 added the Netlist case's procedural posture and the two-front framing with standards-of-review asymmetry. Each round contributes distinct, usable understanding — doctrinal boundaries, drafting implications, empirical design — with limited repetition.

[A|Adaptive Coherence] The sequence builds cumulatively: Round 1's Deere analysis → Round 2's compliance-line follow-up on Deere plus a new enablement thread → Round 3's DRAM specifics plus the eligibility-vs-obviousness distribution question that Round 1's empirical discussion had set up. The Instructor's Round 3 answer explicitly connects back: "the empirical question about obviousness findings is really a question about which front most hardware innovators actually face." User guidance shifts between rounds are tracked (from "recent legal cases" to "legal precedents and implications"), and the final summary consolidates demonstrated contributions without inventing transitions. Minor gap: Round 2's selected question on Amgen was only loosely connected to Round 1's Deere/PTAB focus, though the Instructor bridged them.

[B|Inquiry Relevance] Round 1 directly addressed the prompt with three recent cases (Taction v. Apple, Linden v. ResMed, robotics product liability). Round 2 deepened the precedents-and-implications analysis of the same cases. Round 3's "What else should I know" prompt was answered with the Netlist PTAB case and a three-gate synthesis. All directions serve the stated goal. However, the system never generated its own follow-up questions or redirected based on evidence gaps — it responded to prompts with comprehensive answers rather than pursuing inquiry choices. The scope stayed within patent litigation, missing the right-to-repair, export control, and SEP/FRAND clusters that System A's bootstrap identified as part of the same topic.

[B|Perspective Expansion] Round 2 introduced the "bifurcated legal environment" framing (restrictive on protectability, expansive on damages). Round 3 developed the "three independent gates" model (eligibility, validity, infringement): "Strength at one gate does not guarantee survival at another." This is a useful structural perspective. Round 1 noted the "second wave" strategy (verdict → forward royalties). However, these perspectives are mostly organizational frameworks applied to already-presented cases rather than genuinely new angles on the problem. The product-liability parallel was mentioned but not developed. No hidden assumptions or boundary conditions were investigated.

[B|Evidence-Based Progress] The system consistently tied claims to specific case holdings: Linden's "generic hardware" language, Taction's $5.7B verdict and post-verdict motions, Netlist's substantial-evidence affirmance. Round 3 appropriately flagged uncertainty: "the $5.7 billion figure is not yet a final judgment" and listed uncovered areas (final judgment status, follow-on litigation, legislative developments). Round 1 included a caveat: "this is all patent litigation—I don't have regulatory, antitrust, or product liability cases in the mix." However, the evidence is primarily descriptive of case outcomes rather than used to compare explanations or resolve uncertainties. No source passages were independently verified in this evaluation.

[B|Incremental Value] Round 1 delivered three case summaries with practical implications (component-patent damages scaling, § 101 pleading-stage risk, robotics lifecycle liability). Round 2 added the precedents-established section and a risk-table for prosecutors. Round 3 added the Netlist PTAB case, the three-gate model, and forward-royalty trend analysis. The progression is additive: each round adds distinct cases or frameworks. However, much of Rounds 1-2's content overlaps (both cover Linden and Taction in detail), and the practical lessons in Round 3 ("Draft for eligibility and validity simultaneously," "Freedom-to-operate is essential") are general rather than derived from specific evidence in the record.

[B|Adaptive Coherence] The three rounds form a coherent progression: survey → precedents/implications → additional dimensions. Round 3 explicitly builds on Rounds 1-2: "Beyond the Linden, Taction, and Netlist matters already covered." The three-gate synthesis in Round 3 integrates findings from all prior rounds. The system responded appropriately to the "What else should I know" prompt by adding the PTAB dimension rather than repeating. However, there is no evidence of adaptation to contradictions or new evidence — the system never revised a prior claim or acknowledged a tension between rounds. The final summary consolidates without inventing transitions, which is appropriate.

[C|Inquiry Relevance] Round 1 (General Knowledge Provider) addressed the prompt with three patent cases (Keyless v. Samsung, Gesture Technology Partners, Headwater v. Samsung), explicitly noting "this is all patent litigation—I don't have regulatory, antitrust, or product liability cases." Round 2 shifted to Linden v. ResMed for the precedents-and-implications prompt. Round 3 (Patent litigator) deepened the Linden analysis. The directions are pertinent but narrow — confined to patent eligibility and infringement, missing the broader hardware-innovation legal landscape (right-to-repair, export controls, SEP/FRAND) that the topic encompasses. The system never generated its own follow-up questions; it responded to prompts with answers.

[C|Perspective Expansion] Round 3's Patent litigator developed the waiver trap ("Preserve those positions early, and watch language that invites representative-claim treatment you may later want to contest") and the step-two analysis of why ordered combinations fail. The warm-start dialogue introduced means-plus-function construction (Dyfan), Rule 42(a) consolidation dynamics, B1 designation effects, and MDL lead-case fairness concerns — these are relevant perspectives on hardware litigation. However, within the scored rounds themselves, the perspectives are mostly elaborations of the Linden holding rather than new angles. The warm-start material, while present, is starting context rather than a later exploratory gain.

[C|Evidence-Based Progress] Round 2 cited specific claim language ("internet and networking capable," "physical output display and input transducer") and the Alice step-one/step-two reasoning. Round 3 added the waiver finding ("his counsel agreed Claim 1 is representative") and the specification's admission that the invention "adds communication or remote control features to devices that were already known." Round 1 cited PTAB discretionary denial (Keyless), Supreme Court cert denial (Gesture), and a jury verdict (Headwater). The evidence is well-connected to claims, and Round 1's caveat about scope limitations is appropriately honest. However, the system did not use evidence to compare explanations or resolve uncertainties — it described holdings rather than investigating their implications. Source passages were not independently verified here.

[C|Incremental Value] Round 1 delivered three case summaries with a scope caveat. Round 2 delivered a detailed Linden analysis with drafting takeaways. Round 3 delivered the waiver trap, step-two reasoning, and a "caveat: this is a single case, so I can't confirm a broader trend." Chronologically, Round 2's Linden analysis and Round 3's deeper Linden analysis overlap substantially — Round 3 mostly elaborates Round 2's points with additional detail rather than adding distinct understanding. The warm-start's consolidation/means-plus-function material is present but is starting context. Net distinct contribution across the three rounds is moderate: three cases in Round 1, one case developed across Rounds 2-3.

[C|Adaptive Coherence] Round 1 → Round 2 shifts from a three-case survey to a single-case deep dive (Linden), which is a reasonable response to the changed prompt ("investigate the legal precedents and implications"). Round 3 continues the Linden thread with additional detail, explicitly building on Round 2: "Exactly—and Linden v. ResMed is a telling signal." The progression is cumulative within the Linden analysis. However, Round 1's cases (Keyless, Gesture, Headwater) are never revisited or connected to Rounds 2-3, creating a discontinuity. The system also never adjusted course based on evidence gaps — Round 1's acknowledged limitation ("I don't have regulatory, antitrust, or product liability cases") was not addressed in later rounds.
